title: Hacking the Inference Pareto Frontier - Kyle Kranen, NVIDIA
talk_summary: NVIDIA architect Kyle Kranen explains how to shift the inference Pareto frontier (quality/latency/cost) using disaggregated prefill/decode, KV-cache-aware routing, inference-time scaling (re-querying small models), KV manipulation around tool calls, and worker specialization/autoscaling.

takeaways.technique: Inference-time scaling: re-query a smaller model instead of using a bigger one
takeaways.what_they_do: Re-prompt the same model to reconsider/reason over its result several times; with ~3-4 re-queries an 8B model reaches quality parity with a 49B, and 49B with 235B, at lower cost than the larger model.
takeaways.evidence_quote: with about three or four times of requering, we can see that the 8B model is basically on par with respect to quality as the 49B model
takeaways.numbers: ~3-4x re-query: 8B ≈ 49B quality, 49B ≈ 235B quality; re-querying the small model still cheaper than the large model

takeaways.technique: Route re-queries internally instead of round-tripping to the client
takeaways.what_they_do: When doing inference-time scaling, issue the repeat queries from the router rather than the external client, removing round trips; making the scheduler aware of repeat work adds further benefit.
takeaways.evidence_quote: removing a round trip by making the requeries come from the router instead of coming from the user or the client on the outside allows you to really decrease these round trips

takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of random routing or pure prefix-match routing, minimize a cost function combining prefix match already cached on a node and that node's current load, to avoid queueing on hot nodes.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you actually want to minimize the uh sort of this cost function that includes both the amount of prefix match that you can get from uh or maximize the prefix match
takeaways.numbers: Asymptotically increasing KV cache hit rate as deployment scales, reducing prefill work over time

takeaways.technique: KV manipulation around deterministic tool calls
takeaways.what_they_do: When a tool call takes a known time (e.g. 30s), offload the KV cache to host memory and reload it when the tool is expected to finish, avoiding a second prefill of the same context.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if we have a tool call that takes 30 seconds, the KV is going to be swept out from HPM ... if we know that it's going to be used again, why not just offload it

takeaways.technique: Worker specialization by workload shape (ISL/OSL histogram)
takeaways.what_they_do: Mix aggregated and disaggregated workers, and vary tensor/context parallelism, based on where a request falls in the input/output sequence-length histogram; autoscale prefill vs decode in real time as user distribution shifts.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you actually want to have a mix of aggregated and disagregated workers based on where you are in the OSL ISL histogram
takeaways.numbers: Disaggregation gave up to 2x tokens/sec/GPU at fixed latency on 16 H100s for llama 7B, but little/no gain for low-input-length or extreme low-latency cases
